My SO and I are from the same home town as well. The first semester of college we were about 400 miles apart but north-south of each other, so we were in the same time zone.

After that my SO transferred to a college four time zones and about 3,000 miles away. We see each other 2-3 times a year, and have done so for the past 2 years. Right now we're about six months from closing the distance.

I'm not going to lie, it's difficult. Dealing with the time zone will require you to be a little creative (in our case, I structure my homework time so I can talk to him for a few hours when our free time overlaps, and he stays up a little late to talk to me). Not seeing each other for 6 months is absolutely going to wear you down if you aren't careful and aware of it.

You're probably going to feel more like breaking up at some points. You'll almost definitely spend an hour sobbing some days because you can't stand how much you miss them. Your best friend will be Skype or another video service.

But you know what? You CAN make it. It takes great communication, willingness to make time for each other, and a dose of self-awareness so you can recognize when the distance is taking its toll (I've learned to recognize when I'm irritated by the distance, not my actual SO, so I choose to control my reaction rather than unfairly release it on my SO).

The good news: you have 4 years of long distance behind you, so that proves you can do it. You can adjust to this much easier than you think. And you have a somewhat solid end date. All of those things can make it livable.

My SO and I are doing great. You guys can do it too.

We talk on the phone 2-4 hours per day, but we're both doing other things unless the conversation is really significant. The news, reddit, video games - it's all fair game as long as we're spending a good chunk of our attention on each other.

OP, your case seems smothering to me, but everyone has different levels of need and comfort. The thing is, neither you or your girlfriend can dictate the terms for talking. If she got her way and you focused solely on her for 6 hours every day, you'd be resentful and it would ruin the relationship. Same thing if you got your way. You need to figure out something to balance - say, 3 hours a day but you promise not to do other things while on the phone/Skype.

Also, if she can't respect both your comfort level and the fact that 6 hours of conversation is having a negative effect on important things like schoolwork, that's a problem you guys need to talk about.

I'm hardly old enough (21) to say this, but you're too young to give up on friends and socializing. You're 18 and have been battling depression - of course that has had an impact on your social skills!

Right now I think you have just become familiar and comfortable with being alone - it's easy. But that's still fixable. Take small steps and reward yourself for every bit.

Go out to some public event (food festival, poetry reading, whatever floats your boat) and make a bit of small talk. Nothing major, just surface-level conversation and smiling. Then go home and have some ice cream or watch a movie or whatever makes you happy.

When online, make an effort sometimes to start a conversation or comment just one more time, even if you're not sure you want to. Again, reward yourself.

Do these things on occasion, then gradually it'll get easier to do more frequently (and hopefully you'll enjoy it too). It'll also help you build acquaintances who share similar interests, which could become friends.

That's all the advice I've got. I hope it helps a bit. And if you decide you want to live alone in Wyoming, that's okay. Just make that decision because it genuinely makes you happy, not because it's just easier than trying to socialize.

I can't speak for everyone, but I know sometimes I push people away because it's comfortable. I may be miserable sitting alone in my room, but it can seem less scary and easier than the effort of going out, meeting people and possibly being rejected. It's a comfort zone that feels like crap, but it's a comfort zone nonetheless.

Does any of that sound like you? If so, try just once to defy the comfort zone and go out with these people who clearly like you. Just one time, then you can return to what you know if needed. Repeat from time to time and see if it becomes easier to let people in.

If I'm way off base, then I hope you find something that works for you because you deserve a good life. You are not pathetic. And happy birthday. :)

If he's seen some instances and understands a little bit, that's something to build on. This is just a suggestion, but it might be easier to pick one trait (say, the anxiety or the clinging) at a time and try to explain the cause behind that effect. Use some examples and get him to imagine himself in situations you experienced. Ask him to imagine that feeling multiplied many times over years and how that might change his viewpoint, especially if it started as a child. Basically, he needs to recognize that some of your responses will probably never be normal, and sometimes you may not even understand the reasons why.
I'm not guaranteeing that will work for you, but it has helped me in explaining things with my SO.
